parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Fold (FD)**
> 
> Fold (FD) manufactures cardboard packaging in country M. It employs 190 people and supplies food producers and online retailers.
> 
> Three of FD's largest customers have told it that from 2028 they will buy only from suppliers whose packaging is made entirely from recycled material and who can show that their energy use is falling. Together these three customers provide 44% of FD's revenue.
> 
> FD currently uses 61% recycled material. Moving to 100% would cost around \$2.8m in new equipment.
> 
> Country M's government has also announced a tax on packaging containing less than 70% recycled content, starting in 2027.

Explain **one** reason why sustainability is important to FD.
parts.solution_md:
One reason is that FD's largest customers now treat sustainability as a condition of doing business **[1]**. Three customers providing 44% of FD's revenue will buy only from suppliers using entirely recycled material from 2028, and FD currently uses 61% **[1]**. If FD does not invest the \$2.8m needed to reach 100%, it risks losing nearly half its sales at once, which would cost far more than the equipment, so sustainability has become necessary for FD's survival rather than a choice about its image **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Sustainability matters to a business because of customer requirements, legal and tax changes, cost savings, reputation, and access to finance
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Three customers worth 44% of revenue will require fully recycled packaging from 2028, so failing to invest puts almost half of FD's sales at risk
> - Country M's tax on packaging below 70% recycled content begins in 2027, and FD's current 61% falls below that threshold, adding a cost it does not face today
> - The \$2.8m investment is large, but it answers the customer requirement and the tax at the same time, so the two pressures reinforce one another
> - Being able to prove falling energy use may open opportunities with other buyers applying similar standards, turning compliance into a competitive advantage
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Sustainability is a very broad idea, so narrow it to one strand before you start writing. Trying to cover environmental, social and financial sustainability at once produces a list rather than an explanation. One narrow reason, followed through to its effect on the business, will always score better.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** benefit to a business of a trade agreement between countries.
parts.solution_md:
One benefit is that a trade agreement usually reduces or removes tariffs between the countries involved **[1]**. A tariff is a tax on imports, so removing it lowers the price at which a business can sell its products in the other country **[1]**. Cheaper products are likely to sell in greater numbers, so the business can raise its sales abroad without cutting its own profit margin, and producing those extra units may also lower its average cost **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Trade agreements can reduce tariffs and quotas, simplify customs procedures, standardise regulations, and give businesses more secure access to a partner country's market
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Removing tariffs lowers the selling price in the partner country without reducing the exporter's margin, so sales volumes are likely to rise
> - Simpler customs procedures cut delays and paperwork costs, which matters most for goods that are perishable or time-sensitive
> - Common product standards allow a business to sell the same version of a product in several countries, avoiding the cost of redesigning it for each market
> - More secure access reduces the risk of sudden trade barriers, making it safer to invest in production capacity aimed at export markets
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A benefit question needs you to identify who gains and by what route, not simply to assert that something is good for business. Here the route runs from a lower tariff, to a lower selling price, to higher sales volume. Making that path explicit is what separates a three-mark answer from a one-mark one.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Folio (FL)**
> 
> Folio (FL) is a printing business in country W. It prints books, catalogues and packaging for around 200 customers, and employs 75 people.
> 
> Paper is FL's largest cost. FL buys all of its paper from just two mills, because only these two can supply the weights and finishes its customers require.
> 
> Last year one of the two mills raised its prices by 22% and reduced credit terms from 60 days to 30 days. FL had to pay more, and sooner, than it had planned.
> 
> FL's owner is now considering whether to hold larger stocks of paper or to look for a supplier in another country.

Explain **one** way FL's suppliers can influence its decisions.
parts.solution_md:
One way is that FL's suppliers can dictate the terms on which it buys **[1]**. FL depends on only two mills, because they alone supply the paper weights and finishes its customers need, so when one raised prices by 22% and cut credit from 60 days to 30 days, FL had little choice but to accept **[1]**. Paying more and paying sooner both reduce the cash FL has available, which is exactly why its owner is now weighing up larger stock holdings or a supplier abroad **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Suppliers can influence a business through the prices they charge, their credit terms, their reliability, the quality they provide, and how easily they can be replaced
> 
> AO2
> 
> - FL buys from only two mills because of the specialist weights and finishes required, so its bargaining power is weak and it must largely accept the terms offered
> - A 22% increase on FL's largest cost either squeezes its margins or forces it to raise prices to its 200 customers
> - Cutting credit from 60 days to 30 halves the time FL has to collect money from customers before it must pay the mill, putting pressure on cash flow
> - Supplier behaviour is already reshaping FL's strategy, since the owner is weighing higher stock levels or an overseas supplier, both of which carry costs of their own
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Suppliers can influence a business helpfully or harmfully, and this question asks for one way, not a survey. Choose the direction the case supports, state it plainly, then develop it. Listing price, quality, reliability and delivery without developing any of them will not reach the second and third marks.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** way a government might intervene to help businesses.
parts.solution_md:
One way a government might help businesses is by offering grants or subsidies **[1]**. A grant reduces the amount a business must fund itself when buying equipment or opening a new site, so projects that would otherwise be too expensive become affordable **[1]**. This matters most to smaller firms, which often struggle to borrow, and it can persuade businesses to invest in areas where the government wants new jobs created **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Governments can support businesses through grants and subsidies, tax reductions, training schemes, infrastructure investment, advice services, or reduced regulation
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A grant lowers the amount a firm must fund itself, so investment projects that would be unaffordable become viable
> - Reducing business taxes leaves more profit available for reinvestment, which may encourage expansion and job creation
> - Government-funded training raises the skills available in the labour market, reducing the cost each business must bear to train staff itself
> - Investment in roads, ports or broadband lowers distribution and communication costs for firms across the whole economy
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Without a case study, the development marks still have to be earned, and they come from a chain of reasoning rather than from naming an example. State the intervention, say what it changes for the business, then say what follows from that. Naming a real government scheme adds nothing on its own.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Meadow (MW)**
> 
> Meadow (MW) processes milk into cheese and yoghurt in country K. It employs 340 people at one large plant, where staff work with heavy machinery, hot liquids and refrigerated storage rooms.
> 
> New health and safety laws in country K require all food processing businesses to fit machine guards, provide protective clothing, and give every employee eight hours of safety training each year.
> 
> MW estimates that meeting the new requirements will cost \$620,000 in the first year and \$180,000 a year afterwards.
> 
> In the year before the new law, MW recorded 34 workplace injuries, nine of which required time off work.

Explain **one** way health and safety law affects MW.
parts.solution_md:
One way is that health and safety law increases MW's costs **[1]**. The new requirements mean MW must spend \$620,000 in the first year on machine guards, protective clothing and eight hours of training for each of its 340 employees **[1]**. That money cannot be spent on anything else, such as new production equipment, so in the short term the law reduces the profit MW has available to reinvest, although fewer injuries than last year's 34 should eventually mean less production lost to absence **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Health and safety law places duties on a business to protect its employees, which affects its costs, working practices, productivity and legal risk
> 
> AO2
> 
> - MW must spend \$620,000 in the first year and \$180,000 a year afterwards, money that cannot be used for other investment
> - Eight hours of annual training for 340 employees takes staff away from production while it happens, reducing output during those periods
> - Fewer than last year's 34 injuries should mean less time lost to absence, since nine of them required time off work
> - Failure to comply could bring prosecution, fines or forced closure, which for a single-site business would stop production altogether
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> With a question about law, name the duty the law places on the business first, then follow it through to a business consequence such as cost, output or risk. Answers that describe the legislation in detail but never reach a consequence for the business tend to earn the first mark only.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'environmental audit'.
parts.solution_md:
An environmental audit is a check on the impact a business's activities have on the environment **[1]**, carried out so that the business can measure that impact and identify ways of reducing it **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An assessment of the effect a business has on the environment, covering matters such as emissions, waste and energy use
> - A systematic review of a firm's environmental performance, used to identify where improvements can be made
> - An internal or independent check on how far a business's operations meet the environmental standards it has set or is required to meet

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a term names a process, say both what is examined and what the examination is for. Here that means the effect of the business on the environment, and the purpose of measuring it. A definition that stops at "a check on the environment" leaves the second mark unearned.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'migration'.
parts.solution_md:
Migration is the movement of people from one country or region to another in order to live there **[1]**, which changes the size and make-up of the population in both the place they leave and the place they settle **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The movement of people between countries or regions in order to live and work there
> - People relocating permanently or semi-permanently, altering the population and labour supply of both the origin and the destination
> - Inward and outward movement of population, affecting the number and skills of people available to businesses in an area

> **[exam-tip]**
> Some terms work in both directions, and migration is one of them: people move in and people also move out. A definition mentioning only arrivals describes immigration rather than migration. Where a term is two-sided, check your wording covers both.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'pressure group'.
parts.solution_md:
A pressure group is an organisation formed by people with a shared concern **[1]** that tries to influence the decisions of businesses or governments without seeking to run them **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An organised group of people who campaign to influence the decisions of businesses or governments on a particular issue
> - A body that seeks to change the behaviour of firms or policymakers through campaigning, publicity or lobbying rather than by taking control of them
> - A group with a shared interest that applies public or political pressure in order to change how organisations act

> **[exam-tip]**
> A definition has to fit every example of the term, not just the best-known one. An answer built around a single famous campaign will not describe a local residents' group or a trade body, and both of those count too. Aim for wording that would cover any pressure group you can think of.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'supply-side policy'.
parts.solution_md:
Supply-side policy is government action intended to increase the productive capacity of the economy **[1]** by making markets work more efficiently and improving the quantity or quality of resources such as labour and capital **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Government measures aimed at raising the economy's ability to produce goods and services, rather than at influencing the level of demand
> - Policies designed to improve the efficiency of markets and the quality of labour and capital, such as training schemes, deregulation or tax incentives to invest
> - Action taken to increase long-run productive capacity by improving skills, competition and incentives across the economy

> **[exam-tip]**
> A policy definition must say what the policy is trying to achieve, not just that a government carries it out. Every government policy is government action, so that half earns very little. The mark lies in the purpose: raising the economy's capacity to produce.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'nationalisation'.
parts.solution_md:
Nationalisation is when a government takes ownership of a business or industry **[1]** that was previously owned by private individuals or shareholders **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The transfer of a business or industry from private ownership into public ownership by the state
> - A government buying or taking control of a firm so that it is run by the public sector rather than for private profit
> - The process by which privately owned assets or industries come to be owned and operated by the government

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nationalisation and privatisation describe the same movement in opposite directions, so the mark depends on saying which way ownership travels. "The government gets involved with a business" is too vague; state that ownership moves from private hands into the public sector.

The government's decision to delay payment of business and property taxes was likely the most important policy for UBH's immediate survival **[K] [E]**. Evaluate the likely impact on WTZ’s future profitability of increased focus on corporate social responsibility (CSR).
parts.solution_md:
CSR means a business considers the impact of its decisions on society and the environment **[K]**. One important area where increased CSR could improve WTZ's profitability is the treatment of its employees **[K]**. Currently, many factory workers are paid the minimum wage, work long hours, and face poor conditions, including limited ventilation and no break facilities **[Ap]**. The operations manager has already identified rising absenteeism and a 5% quality rejection rate as serious problems at the Hydrocamel factory **[Ap]**. If WTZ improved working conditions and paid above the minimum wage, employees would be more motivated and less likely to leave, reducing recruitment and training costs **[An]**. Better morale could also reduce absenteeism and raise productivity - and if quality standards improve, the cost of rejected output would fall. Over time, these savings could offset the cost of higher wages, resulting in a net improvement in profitability **[An]**

Increased CSR could also strengthen WTZ's brand image and support revenue growth **[K]**. WTZ already has strong environmental credentials - it recycles plastic waste, manufactures the Hydrocamel to help communities access clean water, and converts waste into electricity **[Ap]**. Kofi believes that actively promoting these activities could build a positive brand identity, which is timely given the PEST analysis shows increasing environmental awareness and the threat of consumer boycotts against businesses that operate unsustainably. For the Hydrocamel, stronger CSR credentials could serve as a USP to differentiate it from the Hippo Barrel competitor launched in 2019 **[Ap]**, helping to win back charities and NGOs that may prefer buying from a more ethical supplier **[An]**. Higher sales volume would increase revenue and, if fixed costs are spread across more units, improve profitability **[An]**

Overall, a genuine focus on CSR is likely to have a positive impact on WTZ's long-term profitability, but the short-term effect will be higher costs **[E]**. This is a concern since WTZ's profit margin has already fallen from 12.8% in 2021 to 9.3% in 2022 **[Ap]**. The biggest gains are most likely to come from improved employee productivity and lower absenteeism, as these directly address existing operational problems that are already costing the business money **[E]**. The reputational benefits of CSR are real but harder to quantify and may take longer to feed through to higher sales. There is also a significant risk. If WTZ promotes CSR credentials while continuing to treat workers poorly, it could face a damaging backlash from the environmental pressure groups highlighted in the PEST analysis **[Ap]**. For CSR to benefit profitability, it must be genuine and applied consistently across the business rather than used selectively as a marketing tool **[E]**
